latin.2632: L. Porro quamvis Scholae Reformatae Doctores in eo conveniant gratiam non tantum in hominis mentem, sed etiam in voluntatem efficaciam suam exerere, eamque potenter & infallibiliter ad bonum flectere & determinare: inter eos tamen est aliquis dissensus de modo quo gratia voluntatem nostram movet, ut in Deum feratur, & bono consentiat.
latin.2633: LI. Nam Paulus Testardus, & Moses Amyraldus, aliique qui cum iis in gratiae negotio Cameronis Methodum & doctrinam sequuntur, efficaciam gratiae divinae, quae hominem ad Deum convertit, eique fidem in Christum ingenerat, & Dei amore cor illius accendit, in eo consistere docent, quod salutaris veritas in Evangelio proposita eo modo menti offeratur, & arcana virtute spiritus mens intus ita disponatur, ut homo firmissimam & efficacissimam veritatis illius persuasionem inde concipiat, statuatque nihil melius, & ad veram beatitudinem obtinendam conducibilius, quam ut quis Christo adhaereat, & Evangelio illius obsequatur. Unde fit ut voluntas, quae ex eorum hypothesi, necessario sequitur ductum & judicium intellectus practici, bonum illud salutare per Evangelium oblatum, & ab intellectu monstratum suscipiat, atque avide complectatur: & sic a rebus vanis & terrenis aversa tota convertatur ad Deum, qua in re consistit ejus innovatio & sanctificatio.
latin.2634: LII. Adeoque volunt illi efficaciam gratiae divinae primario & immediate in solam mentem sese exerere, in affectus autem atque voluntatem consequenter solum & secundario: sic ut renovatio voluntatis & affectuum non fiat, nisi mediante intellectus renovatione, dum ad eas facultates, intellectus ductui subjectas, lucis mentem renovantis fructus & ἐνέργεια pervenit. Ut videre est apud Paulum Testardum in Irenico thesi 424. & sequentibus.
latin.2635: LIII. Ex dictis vero patet eorum sententiam non parum discrepare ab opinione illorum qui sentiunt totam gratiae efficaciam sitam esse in morali quadam suasione, quae voluntatem relinquat in indifferentia, & possit ab illa rejici, vel admitti. In iis enim qui per Dei gratiam convertuntur, non solum agnoscunt quandam spiritus Dei per verbum operantis suasionem, sed vehementem plane & fortem persuasionem, quae voluntatem secum rapit & efficacissime movet, ac suavissime quidem, sed certo tamen & infallibiliter ad bonum determinat, & consensum ab ea exprimit, non vero tanquam a dubia & indifferenti expectat.
latin.2636: LIV. Verum alii Scholae Reformatae Theologi volunt immediatam gratiae operationem non solum mentem attingere, dum eam illuminat, & nova luce perfundit, sed ipsam quoque voluntatem, in qua consensum illum, quem divinis monitis adhibet, realiter & Physice operatur.
latin.2637: LV. Hanc sententiam tradit & explicat Amesius in Bellarmino enervato libro tertio de Gratia capite tertio. Nos dicimus, inquit, una cum suasione morali conjungi etiam realem efficientiam Dei, qua novum principium spiritualis vitae cordi hominis efficaciter vocati ingeneratur, & homo simul excitatur ad hujus vitae actus eliciendos.
latin.2638: LVI. Ibidemque omnino probat, & ut suam agnoscit sententiam Didaci Alvarés, quae est, Deum per auxilium gratiae efficax Physice, sive ad modum causae Physicae praedeterminare arbitrium creatum, ut infallibiliter consentiat & cooperetur Deo vocanti atque excitanti. Posteaque ipsius Alvarés verbis utens, dicit Physice praedeterminare nihil aliud esse, quam vere, efficienter, vel realiter facere, ut ipsum arbitrium infallibiliter Deo cooperetur. Et Auxilium gratiae ex se efficax, prout venit a Deo antecedenter ad liberam cooperationem arbitrii, & auxilium Physice praedeterminans idem significare.
latin.2639: LVII. Quantumcunque vero tum hi tum illi Scholae Reformatae Doctores efficaciam gratiae divinae exaggerent, nolunt tamen illam quicquam humanae voluntatis libertati praejudicare, sed quaecunque bona opera per Dei gratiam ab homine fiunt, ab iis libere fieri, adeoque primum ipsum actum conversionis non minus liberum esse, quam qui eum sequuntur, nec solum esse vitalem voluntatis nostrae operationem, sed ab ea libere elici.
latin.2640: LVIII. Quomodo vero ista inter se constent, non eadem ratione omnes ostendere conantur. Et quidem modo citatus Amesius sic post Didacum Alvarés conciliare nititur immediatam illam & efficacem gratiae divinae in voluntatem operationem & determinationem, cum voluntatis ipsius libertate in agendo, & gratiae obsequendo. Nempe libere operari dicit illum qui dum agit retinet potestatem non agendi. Jam vero gratiam, quamvis voluntatem moveat & determinet ad agendum, ab ea tamen non tollere non agendi potestatem. Quippe potentiam ad non operandum simul consistere in eodem subjecto cum gratia & auxilio quod requiritur ad operandum, & efficit ut aliquis operetur: licet simul nunquam sint nec esse possint in eodem subjecto gratia & auxilium ad talem operationem particularem datum, & carentia talis actus. Quod alii dicunt gratiam actum quidem determinare, sed tamen a facultate non tollere omnem indifferentiam & indeterminationem.
latin.2641: LIX. Illi vero priores qui Cameronis doctrinam sequuntur, ex sua hypothesi, non difficulter ostendi posse putant quomodo certa & infallibilis, & a voluntatis nostrae consensu minime dependens gratiae operatio cum libertate humana optime consentiat. Nam juxta eorum doctrinam, certa & infallibilis est illa operatio, quoniam mens rite affecta, & sese habens naturae congruenter, non potest verum oblatum & agnitum non amplecti, & non judicare bonum id cujus bonitas ipsi in aperto ponitur: quandoquidem ex convenienti appulsu & applicatione objecti ad facultatem, quae recte se habet, necessario sequitur operatio naturae conveniens. Et similiter voluntas non potest non velle & sequi id quod, omnibus expensis, intellectus volendum & sequendum judicat.
latin.2642: LX. Neque tamen quicquam hic officit libertati, sive ex parte intellectus, sive ex parte voluntatis. Non ex parte intellectus, quia erga ipsum gratia haec duo tantum praestat, primo ut Evangelica veritas in convenienti luce ipsi proponatur: Deinde ut in statum congruentem restituatur, aut etiam aliquantum supra naturae sortem evehatur. Licet autem intellectus non possit vero agnito assensum non praebere, nulla tamen vis ipsi a proposita veritate affertur, dum assentitur vero, & in eo naturae suae maxime congruenter agit: ac proinde si qua species libertatis ipsi competit, hac in parte nihil laeditur. Et multo minus interna gratiae operatio, quae aut amissas vires intellectui restituit, aut etiam novas sufficit, praejudicare potest libertati intellectus, si quam habere censetur.
latin.2643: LXI. Ex parte vero voluntatis, quanquam quae descripta est gratiae operatio, necessario ejus consensum eliciat, nullatenus tamen illi libertatem adimit. Nec enim voluntatem movet, & determinat, nisi per intellectus practici judicium. Sed ex virorum illorum doctorum sententia, necessitas & determinatio actuum voluntatis, quae ex mentis practicae judicio oritur, non obstat quominus libere a voluntate procedant: quandoquidem libertas voluntatis non opponitur cuivis necessitati, sed illi tantum, quae est a vi externa, a materia, vel a sensu. Quae latius diducta videre est apud Mosen Amyraldum tractatu de libero arbitrio, praecipue Sectione quarta. Et similiter in libro posthumo Josuae Placei de eodem argumento.
latin.2644: LXII. Sed vetustiores Scholae Reformatae Doctores simplicius respondent gratiam non tollere a voluntate libertatem, licet aliquam ei necessitatem imponat, quia non omnis necessitas cum libertate pugnat, sed ea solum quae est a vi externa, vel a naturali determinatione. Gratia vero voluntatem non cogit, neque vim ei ullam affert, sed illam suaviter flectit, & modo qui est ejus naturae consentaneus.
latin.2645: LXIII. Porro quod fatentur Scholae Reformatae Doctores, hominem qui per Dei gratiam convertitur, libere ipsum primum conversionis actum elicere, prima specie satis concordare non videtur, cum eo quod communiter docent, idque cum Theologis confessionis Augustanae, videlicet, hominem ad opus regenerationis & conversionis suae mere passive se habere. Quomodo enim voluntas humana potest conversionis actum libere elicere, & simul tamen ad sui conversionem mere passive se habere? an mere passive se habet voluntas quae supponitur libere operari?
latin.2646: LXIV. Hunc nodum solvunt Theologi Britanni in explicatione suae sententiae circa tertium & quartum articulum, actis Synodi Dordrechtanae inserta. Ubi observant conversionem duplici sensu sumi. Et primo quidem denotare immediatum opus Dei hominem regenerantis. Secundo denotare actionem hominis per fidem & poenitentiam salutiferam se ad Deum convertentis. Ad opus conversionis, sive regenerationis primo modo sumptae homo, juxta ipsos, se habet passive, neque est in potestate voluntatis humanae impedire Deum sic immediate convertentem & regenerantem. In conversione vero secundo modo accepta voluntas acta a Deo agit, actusque, quibus constat nostra ad Deum conversio, elicit.
latin.2647: LXV. Caeterum conversionem prout immediatum opus Dei designat, dicunt esse qua Deus animos electorum suorum prius variis actibus gratiae suae excitatos & praeparatos, intima quadam, & mirabili operatione regenerat, & quasi de novo creat; infundendo spiritum vivificantem & omnes animae facultates novis qualitatibus imbuendo. Hanc vero conversionem, ex eorum sensu, sequitur, non tempore sed natura, nostra conversio actualis, Deo proliciente ipsum actum credendi & convertendi ex mutata voluntate, quo acta a Deo agit & ipsa, convertendo se ad Deum & credendo, hoc est, actum suum vitalem eliciendo. Addunt divinam illam actionem non laedere voluntatis libertatem, sed roborare: nec extirpare radicitus vitiosam resistendi possibilitatem; sed efficaciter & suaviter dare homini firmam obediendi voluntatem.
latin.2648: LXVI. Eodem redit quod docent Theologi Hassiaci in expositione suae sententiae circa articulum tertium & quartum, quae inserta quoque est actis ejusdem synodi. Ibi enim sic se habet eorum sexta thesis de homine in statu gratiae. Voluntas itaque hominis ad qualitates, seu facultates & vires supernaturales, nec non ad inclinationes novas recipiendas, habet se mere passive; ita ut actio Spiritus Sancti supernaturales illas vires in voluntatem infundentis, eandemque efficaciter & potenter ad conversionem & fidem flectentis & inclinantis, non a voluntate humana, ejusque cooperatione, vel consensu pendeat: Ad ipsos vero fidei, charitatis, spei, &c. actus, motusque bonos, non pure passive, sed passive & active se habet: cum Dei gratia praeveniente acta & mota, ac subsequente adjuta, ipsa etiam agat, fideique, charitatis, spei, aliarumque virtutum actus producat. Atque hinc non Deus in nobis, seu per nos, sed nos gratia Dei credere, sperare, diligere dicimur.

sections.title: The Reformed differ on how grace moves the will
sections.pass_a: L. Further, although the Doctors of the Reformed School agree in this, that grace exerts its efficacy not only on the mind of man, but also on the will, and bends & determines it powerfully & infallibly to good: yet among them there is some disagreement about the manner in which grace moves our will, so that it may be carried toward God, & consent to the good.
pass_b: Thesis L. Further, the teachers of the Reformed school all agree that grace exerts its efficacy not just on the human mind but on the will as well, and that it bends and settles the will toward the good with power and without fail.
Where they part company is over how grace moves our will so that it turns toward God and gives its assent to what is good.

sections.title: Testard, Amyraut and Camero's followers: grace works by persuading the mind
sections.pass_a: LI. For Paulus Testardus, & Moses Amyraldus, and others who with them follow the Method & doctrine of Camero in the matter of grace, teach that the efficacy of divine grace, which converts man to God, and begets in him faith in Christ, & kindles his heart with the love of God, consists in this, that the saving truth set forth in the Gospel is offered to the mind in such a way, & the mind is inwardly so disposed by the secret power of the spirit, that man thence conceives a most firm & most efficacious persuasion of that truth, and determines that nothing is better, & more conducive to obtaining true blessedness, than that one cleave to Christ, & obey his Gospel. Whence it comes about that the will, which on their hypothesis necessarily follows the lead & judgment of the practical intellect, takes up that saving good offered through the Gospel, & shown by the intellect, and eagerly embraces it: & so, turned away from vain & earthly things, it is wholly converted to God, in which consists its renewal & sanctification.
pass_b: Thesis LI. Paulus Testardus, Moses Amyraldus and the others who follow Camero's method and teaching on grace hold that the efficacy of God's grace, which turns a person to God, plants faith in Christ in him and sets his heart on fire with love for God, works like this. The saving truth set out in the Gospel is presented to the mind in a certain way, and the Spirit's hidden power so shapes the mind from within that the person comes to be utterly and effectively convinced of that truth.

He concludes that nothing is better, and nothing does more to bring a person to true happiness, than holding fast to Christ and obeying his Gospel. On their premise the will must follow where the practical intellect leads and what it judges, so the will takes up the saving good that the Gospel offers and the intellect points out, and grasps it eagerly. Turned away from empty and earthly things, it turns wholly to God, and in this its renewal and sanctification consist.

sections.title: On this view grace reaches the will only through the mind
sections.pass_a: LII. And so they hold that the efficacy of divine grace exerts itself primarily & immediately on the mind alone, but on the affections and will only consequently & secondarily: so that the renewal of the will & of the affections does not take place, except by means of the renewal of the intellect, while the fruit & ἐνέργεια (working) of the light renewing the mind reaches those faculties, which are subject to the lead of the intellect. As may be seen in Paulus Testardus in the Irenicum thesis 424. & following.
pass_b: Thesis LII. So they hold that the efficacy of God's grace exerts itself first and directly on the mind alone, and on the affections and the will only as a result and at second hand. The will and affections are renewed only through the renewing of the intellect, as the fruit and working (energeia) of the light that renews the mind passes on to those faculties, which are subject to the intellect's lead.
This can be seen in Paulus Testardus, Irenicum, thesis 424 and following.

sections.title: This differs from mere moral suasion
sections.pass_a: LIII. But from what has been said it is plain that their opinion differs not a little from the opinion of those who think that the whole efficacy of grace is placed in a certain moral suasion, which leaves the will in indifference, & can be rejected or admitted by it. For in those who are converted through the grace of God, they acknowledge not only a certain suasion of the spirit of God working through the word, but a plainly vehement & strong persuasion, which carries the will away with it & moves it most efficaciously, and most sweetly indeed, but yet certainly & infallibly determines it to good, & draws out consent from it, not however awaits it as from a will doubtful & indifferent.
pass_b: Thesis LIII. It is clear from this that their view is quite different from that of people who place the whole efficacy of grace in a kind of moral persuasion, one that leaves the will undecided and can be either accepted or rejected by it.

In those who are converted by God's grace they recognize not only some persuading by God's Spirit working through the word, but a truly forceful and strong persuasion that sweeps the will along and moves it with the greatest effect: very gently indeed, yet surely and without fail it settles the will on the good and draws its consent out of it, instead of waiting for consent as if from a will still doubtful and undecided.

sections.title: Other Reformed: grace works in the will itself
sections.pass_a: LIV. But other Theologians of the Reformed School hold that the immediate operation of grace not only touches the mind, while it illuminates it, & floods it with new light, but also the will itself, in which it works really & Physically that consent, which it gives to the divine admonitions.
pass_b: Thesis LIV. Other theologians of the Reformed school, however, hold that grace acts directly not only on the mind, enlightening it and flooding it with new light, but on the will itself as well.
In the will, they say, grace really and physically produces the consent that the will gives to God's admonitions.

sections.title: Ames: a real working of God joined to moral suasion
sections.pass_a: LV. This opinion Amesius hands down & explains in Bellarminus enervatus book three on Grace chapter three. We say, he says, that together with moral suasion there is joined also a real efficiency of God, by which a new principle of spiritual life is begotten in the heart of a man efficaciously called, & the man at the same time is stirred up to elicit the acts of this life.
pass_b: Thesis LV. Amesius sets out and explains this view in Bellarminus enervatus, book 3, on grace, chapter 3. 'We say,' he writes, 'that along with moral persuasion there is also a real causal working of God.
By it a new source of spiritual life is planted in the heart of the person who is effectively called, and at the same time he is roused to perform the acts of this life.'

sections.title: Ames adopts Alvarez on physical predetermination
sections.pass_a: LVI. And in the same place he entirely approves, & acknowledges as his own the opinion of Didacus Alvarez, which is, that God through the efficacious help of grace Physically, or after the manner of a Physical cause, predetermines the created will, so that it infallibly consents & cooperates with God calling and stirring up. And afterwards using the words of Alvarez himself, he says that to predetermine Physically is nothing else, than truly, efficiently, or really to bring it about that the will itself infallibly cooperates with God. And that help of grace efficacious of itself, as it comes from God antecedently to the free cooperation of the will, & help Physically predetermining, signify the same.
pass_b: Thesis LVI. In the same place he fully approves Didacus Alvarez's view and owns it as his own: through the efficacious help of grace God physically predetermines the created will, that is, in the manner of a physical cause, so that it consents without fail and works together with God as he calls and rouses it.

Then, in Alvarez's own words, he says that to predetermine physically is nothing other than truly, efficiently or really to make the will itself work together with God without fail. He adds that 'help of grace efficacious of itself', as it comes from God ahead of the will's free cooperation, and 'help that predetermines physically' mean the same thing.

sections.title: Both parties keep the will's freedom
sections.pass_a: LVII. But however much both these and those Doctors of the Reformed School magnify the efficacy of divine grace, yet they will not have it prejudice in any way the freedom of the human will, but whatever good works are done by man through the grace of God, are done by them freely, and accordingly the first act of conversion itself is no less free, than those which follow it, and is not only a vital operation of our will, but is freely elicited by it.
pass_b: Thesis LVII. Yet however much both groups of Reformed teachers stress the efficacy of God's grace, they deny that it in any way harms the freedom of the human will. Whatever good works a person does by God's grace, he does freely.
So the very first act of conversion is just as free as the acts that follow it: it is not merely a living operation of our will but one the will freely brings forth.

sections.title: Ames' reconciliation: the power not to act remains
sections.pass_a: LVIII. But how these things agree with each other, not all try to show in the same way. And indeed Amesius, just cited, after Didacus Alvarez thus strives to reconcile that immediate & efficacious operation & determination of divine grace on the will, with the freedom of the will itself in acting, & in obeying grace. Namely he says that he operates freely who while he acts retains the power of not acting. Now grace, although it moves & determines the will to act, yet does not take from it the power of not acting. For the power to not operate exists at the same time in the same subject with the grace & help which is required for operating, & brings it about that someone operates: although there never are nor can be at the same time in the same subject the grace & help given for such a particular operation, & the lack of such an act. Which others express by saying that grace determines the act indeed, but yet does not take away from the faculty all indifference & indetermination.
pass_b: Thesis LVIII. Not all of them, however, show in the same way how these things fit together. Amesius, just cited, following Didacus Alvarez, tries to reconcile that direct and effective working and determining of God's grace in the will with the will's own freedom in acting and in obeying grace.

He says that someone acts freely if, while acting, he keeps the power not to act. Grace moves and determines the will to act, yet it does not take away its power not to act. The power not to act exists in the same subject together with the grace and help needed for acting, the help that makes someone act.

Yet the grace and help given for a particular action and the absence of that action never are, and never can be, in the same subject at once. Others say the same thing this way: grace does determine the act, but it does not remove all indifference and indetermination from the faculty.

sections.title: The Cameronians: certainty from the mind's nature
sections.pass_a: LIX. But those former, who follow the doctrine of Camero, think it can be shown without difficulty from their hypothesis how the certain & infallible operation of grace, depending in no way on the consent of our will, agrees very well with human freedom. For according to their doctrine, that operation is certain & infallible, because the mind rightly affected, & disposed agreeably to its nature, cannot not embrace the truth offered & known, & not judge good that whose goodness is set openly before it: since from the fitting approach & application of the object to the faculty, which is rightly disposed, there necessarily follows an operation agreeable to its nature. And similarly the will cannot not will & follow that which, all things weighed, the intellect judges to be willed & followed.
pass_b: Thesis LIX. The first group, Camero's followers, think their premise makes it easy to show how a working of grace that is sure and infallible, and in no way depends on our will's consent, fits perfectly with human freedom.

On their teaching that working is sure and infallible because a mind in the right state, acting in keeping with its nature, cannot fail to embrace the truth when it is offered and recognized, or fail to judge good what is plainly shown to be good. When an object is fittingly brought to bear on a faculty that is in good order, an action in keeping with its nature follows by necessity.
In the same way the will cannot fail to will and follow what the intellect, having weighed everything, judges is to be willed and followed.

sections.title: The Cameronians: no harm to the intellect's freedom
sections.pass_a: LX. Nor yet does anything here hinder freedom, whether on the part of the intellect, or on the part of the will. Not on the part of the intellect, because toward it grace performs only these two things, first that the Evangelical truth be set before it in a fitting light: Next that it be restored to a fitting state, or even be raised somewhat above the lot of nature. And although the intellect cannot refuse assent to the truth known, yet no force is brought on it by the truth set forth, while it assents to the truth, & in that acts most agreeably to its nature: and therefore if any kind of freedom belongs to it, in this respect it is in no way hurt. And much less can the internal operation of grace, which either restores lost powers to the intellect, or even supplies new ones, prejudice the freedom of the intellect, if it is thought to have any.
pass_b: Thesis LX. Nothing here harms freedom, they say, either in the intellect or in the will. Not in the intellect, since grace does only two things for it: it sets the Gospel truth before it in a fitting light, and it restores it to a fitting condition, or even lifts it somewhat above its natural lot.

The intellect cannot withhold assent from a truth it has recognized, but the truth put before it does it no violence when it assents, since in assenting it acts entirely in keeping with its nature. So if the intellect has any sort of freedom, that freedom suffers no harm here.
Still less can the inward working of grace, which gives back to the intellect the powers it had lost or even supplies new ones, damage whatever freedom the intellect is thought to have.

sections.title: The Cameronians: no harm to the will's freedom
sections.pass_a: LXI. But on the part of the will, although the operation of grace that has been described necessarily elicits its consent, yet it in no way takes away its freedom. For it does not move & determine the will, except through the judgment of the practical intellect. But in the opinion of those learned men, the necessity & determination of the acts of the will, which arises from the practical judgment of the mind, does not prevent their proceeding freely from the will: since freedom of the will is not opposed to every necessity, but only to that which is from external force, from matter, or from sense. Which may be seen set out more broadly in Moses Amyraldus' treatise on free will, especially Section four. And similarly in the posthumous book of Josua Placeus on the same subject.
pass_b: Thesis LXI. As for the will, the working of grace described above does necessarily draw out its consent, yet it in no way takes its freedom away, since it moves and determines the will only through the judgment of the practical intellect.

In these learned men's view, the necessity and determination of the will's acts that come from the mind's practical judgment do not stop those acts from proceeding freely from the will. The will's freedom is not opposed to every necessity, only to necessity that comes from outside force, from matter or from the senses.
This is argued more fully in Moses Amyraldus' treatise on free will, especially section 4, and likewise in Josua Placeus' posthumous book on the same subject.

sections.title: The older Reformed answer more simply
sections.pass_a: LXII. But the older Doctors of the Reformed School answer more simply that grace does not take away freedom from the will, although it imposes some necessity on it, because not every necessity conflicts with freedom, but only that which is from external force, or from natural determination. But grace does not compel the will, nor brings any force on it, but bends it sweetly, & in a manner which is agreeable to its nature.
pass_b: Thesis LXII. The older teachers of the Reformed school give a simpler answer. Grace does not take freedom away from the will, even though it lays a certain necessity on it, because not every necessity is at odds with freedom, only the necessity that comes from outside force or from natural determination.
Grace does not compel the will or do it any violence; it bends it gently, in a way that suits its nature.

sections.title: A difficulty: free first act, yet merely passive
sections.pass_a: LXIII. Further, what the Doctors of the Reformed School confess, that the man who is converted through the grace of God freely elicits the first act of conversion itself, at first sight does not seem to agree well enough with what they commonly teach, and that with the Theologians of the Augsburg confession, namely, that man stands merely passively toward the work of his regeneration & conversion. For how can the human will freely elicit the act of conversion, & yet at the same time stand merely passively toward its own conversion? or does the will stand merely passively that is supposed to operate freely?
pass_b: Thesis LXIII. The Reformed teachers also admit that a person converted by God's grace freely performs the very first act of conversion. At first sight this does not seem to fit well with what they commonly teach, in agreement with the theologians of the Augsburg Confession: that in the work of his regeneration and conversion a person is merely passive.
How can the human will freely perform the act of conversion and yet be merely passive in its own conversion? Can a will that is assumed to act freely be merely passive?

sections.title: The British theologians: conversion in two senses
sections.pass_a: LXIV. This knot the British Theologians untie in the explanation of their opinion on the third & fourth article, inserted in the acts of the Synod of Dort. Where they observe that conversion is taken in a twofold sense. And first indeed that it denotes the immediate work of God regenerating man. Secondly that it denotes the action of man converting himself to God through faith & saving repentance. Toward the work of conversion, or regeneration taken in the first way man, according to them, stands passively, nor is it in the power of the human will to hinder God thus immediately converting & regenerating. But in conversion taken in the second way the will, moved by God, acts, and elicits the acts in which our conversion to God consists.
pass_b: Thesis LXIV. The British theologians untie this knot in the explanation of their opinion on the third and fourth articles that is included in the Acts of the Synod of Dort. They point out that 'conversion' is used in two senses.

First, it means the direct work of God by which he regenerates a person; second, the act by which a person turns himself to God through faith and saving repentance. In conversion or regeneration in the first sense, on their account, a person is passive, and it is not in the human will's power to hinder God as he thus directly converts and regenerates.
In conversion in the second sense the will, moved by God, does act, and it performs the acts that make up our turning to God.

sections.title: The British theologians: regeneration first, then our act of faith
sections.pass_a: LXV. Moreover conversion as it designates the immediate work of God, they say is that by which God regenerates the souls of his elect, first stirred up & prepared by various acts of his grace, by a certain inmost, & wonderful operation, & as it were creates them anew; by infusing the life-giving spirit & imbuing all the faculties of the soul with new qualities. But this conversion, in their sense, is followed, not in time but in nature, by our actual conversion, God drawing forth the very act of believing & of converting out of the changed will, whereby, moved by God, it acts itself too, by converting itself to God & believing, that is, by eliciting its own vital act. They add that that divine action does not hurt the freedom of the will, but strengthens it: nor roots out by the roots the vicious possibility of resisting; but efficaciously & sweetly gives to man a firm will to obey.
pass_b: Thesis LXV. Conversion in the sense of God's direct work, they say, is the work by which God, through an innermost and wonderful working, regenerates the souls of his elect, which various acts of his grace have already stirred and prepared, and as it were creates them anew, pouring in the life-giving Spirit and filling every faculty of the soul with new qualities.

In their view this conversion is followed, not in time but in order of nature, by our actual conversion: God draws the act of believing and turning out of the changed will, and the will, moved by God, then acts too, turning itself to God and believing, that is, producing its own living act.

They add that this divine action does not damage the will's freedom but strengthens it. It does not tear out by the roots the corrupt possibility of resisting, but effectively and gently gives the person a firm will to obey.

sections.title: The Hessian theologians teach the same
sections.pass_a: LXVI. To the same comes what the Hessian Theologians teach in the exposition of their opinion on the third & fourth article, which is also inserted in the acts of the same synod. For there their sixth thesis on man in the state of grace runs thus. The will of man therefore stands merely passively toward receiving supernatural qualities, or faculties & powers, and also new inclinations; so that the action of the Holy Spirit infusing those supernatural powers into the will, and efficaciously & powerfully bending & inclining it to conversion & faith, does not depend on the human will, and its cooperation, or consent: But toward the very acts of faith, charity, hope, &c., and good motions, it stands not purely passively, but passively & actively: since, moved & stirred by preventing grace of God, and helped by subsequent grace, it also itself acts, and produces the acts of faith, charity, hope, and the other virtues. And hence not God in us, or through us, but we by the grace of God are said to believe, to hope, to love.
pass_b: Thesis LXVI. The Hessian theologians teach the same thing in the exposition of their opinion on the third and fourth articles, which is also included in the Acts of that Synod. Their sixth thesis, on man in the state of grace, reads:

'The human will is therefore merely passive in receiving supernatural qualities, or faculties and powers, and new inclinations. The action of the Holy Spirit, who pours those supernatural powers into the will and bends and inclines it effectively and powerfully to conversion and faith, does not depend on the human will or on its cooperation or consent.

But with respect to the acts of faith, love, hope and so on, and to good motions, the will is not purely passive but both passive and active. Moved and stirred by God's preceding grace and helped by his following grace, it acts too, and produces acts of faith, love, hope and the other virtues. That is why it is not said that God believes, hopes and loves in us or through us, but that we do so by God's grace.'
